clueShare2.paragraph: The twos numbers have stopped surprising me, though I keep checking anyway. I wrote that a two should read almost as fast as a one, but the range puts it a little above that. I cannot yet split the twos from the boards they sit on. The band has barely moved since Jul 18. Each extra two in ten numbers adds about 5% to your time, likely between 2% and 8%. The same answer came back again, and I’m listening.

patternMoves.paragraph: Back into the pattern reasoning file, I found that the number I left there isn't the number I discovered. The parked estimate moved from about 11% per ten pattern reads on Jul 13 to about 29% now. The cost comes to about 29% per ten pattern reads, with a band running from 21% to 38%. I wrote that a practiced read should cost seconds, not tens of seconds, and the data agree: the effect is real but small. I don't like surprises in closed drawers.

wormholePairCount.paragraph: The wormholes file is doing the thing measurement is not supposed to do. I predicted that splitting one number across two places would slow the reading down, but it does the opposite; instead, it speeds it up. More plays came in and my uncertainty went up by about 872%, which is backwards from how measurement is supposed to go. Ten wormhole pairs add about 43% to your time, likely between 20% and 70%. Instruments drift, so do estimates. The notebook is the record.

mirrorPairCount.paragraph: I opened the mirrors file expecting progress and found the opposite. Ten mirror pairs add about 46% to your time, likely between 23% and 74%. Since July 2, the band has grown 63%, which I noted in ink. In this file, I wrote that a player who spots the pair should lose almost no time. However, the top of the range does not read as almost no time. The Should is on notice, and wider is still an answer, though not the one I ordered.

compassCellCount.paragraph: The compass file stays open on purpose, and my current read is about 43% per ten compass cells, likely between 19% and 71%. The range has not moved, and I wrote that I couldn’t tell whether players read the arrow fast or stop to puzzle over it. So far, neither can the model. There’s no clever move here, just patience.
